title: Let That Mongo!
bodyHtml:
Mongo (also known as Nkundo or Lomongo) is a Bantu language spoken by the Mongo Peoples of the central Democratic Republic of the Congo. Presently, there are around 400,000 native speakers spread out over a large area around the Congo River.

Below is a table showing a few verb conjugations in Lomongo. [d͡ʒ] is a consonant pronounced like the [j] in the English word jump. [ŋ] is a consonant pronounced like the [ng] at the end of the English word sing.

Imperative2nd singular3rd singular3rd pluralEnglish
botaootaaotabaota‘beget’ (to give rise to; to bring about)
kambaokambaakambabakamba‘work’
imed͡ʒawimed͡ʒaimed͡ʒabimed͡ʒa‘consent’
usawusausabusa‘throw’
bataoataaatabaata‘get’
ɛnawɛnaɛnabɛna‘see’
isawisaisabisa‘hide’
d͡ʒilaod͡ʒilaad͡ʒilabad͡ʒila‘wait’
inawinainabina‘hate’
binaoinaainabaina‘dance’
asawasaasabasa‘search’
saŋgaosaŋgaasaŋgabasaŋga‘say’

A1. Explain how these Mongo verb forms work by filling in the blanks below.

Each Mongo verb has a root form. The 4 verb forms shown here are formed by adding a prefix before the root form. The prefix for the imperative form is , the prefix for the 2nd singular form is , the prefix for the 3rd singular form is , and the prefix for the 3rd plural form is . (Note that some of these prefixes may be empty; to note this, write the symbol Ø-).

However, we are not done yet: to get the final verb form, we must apply some sound change rules. The relevant rules are:

  1. If there are two , in a row, delete .
  2. Delete when it appears between two .
  3. Change to when it appears before a .

There is one final wrinkle: the order that these rules are applied in matters. The rules must be applied in this order: First apply rule , then rule , then rule .

hints.text: Start with rows whose imperative begins with a consonant that is not b, such as 'work' (kamba) or 'say' (saŋga). In those rows nothing seems to get lost, so you can read the three person markers straight off the front of the words.

Now compare rows whose imperative begins with a vowel and rows whose imperative begins with b. Three small adjustments are at work: two vowels next to each other cannot both survive, a b between two vowels disappears, and o and w are two shapes of the same sound (one appears before a vowel, the other before a consonant). The tricky part is deciding which adjustment happens first, since applying them in a different order can give a different result.

Try the given row for 'search': imperative asa, 2nd singular wasa. Attaching the 2nd-singular marker to asa puts two vowels side by side. If you collapsed those two vowels first you would just get asa back, which is not the printed form, so the other adjustment has to happen before the collapsing rule. Tracing it in that order gives wasa. Use the same reasoning to decide where the b-deletion rule belongs by testing the given row for 'get' (bata, aata).

explanationHtml:
What we are looking for

Each verb has a root (the bare meaning-carrying part). The four columns are built by putting a small piece, a prefix, in front of the root. But the printed forms are not always just prefix + root: some sounds get squeezed out or changed when the two pieces meet. That is what the rules in A1 describe.

Step 1: read the prefixes off the easy rows

Pick a row where the imperative starts with a consonant other than b, for example ‘work’:

  • imperative kamba
  • 2nd singular okamba
  • 3rd singular akamba
  • 3rd plural bakamba

The imperative is the bare root, so the imperative prefix is empty (written Ø-). The other three columns simply add o-, a- and ba-. The row for ‘say’ (saŋga, osaŋga, asaŋga, basaŋga) confirms this.

Step 2: what happens when the root starts with a vowel

Look at ‘hide’: root isa. The 3rd singular is isa, not aisa: a + isa has two vowels in a row, and the first one drops. The 3rd plural is bisa, not baisa: in ba + isa the a and the i are again next to each other, and again the first one goes. That is Rule 1: if there are two vowels in a row, delete the first one.

The 2nd singular is wisa. Here o + isa did not simply lose its o; the o turned into w. Compare okamba (o before a consonant) with wisa, wusa, wɛna, wasa (o before a vowel). So Rule 3: change o to w before a vowel.

Step 3: what happens when the root starts with b

Look at ‘dance’: imperative bina, 3rd plural baina. The prefix ba- plus the root bina should give babina, but the second b has vanished, leaving a-i as neighbours. Same in ‘get’: a + bata gives aata, and o + bata gives oata. In every case the missing sound sat between two vowels. That is Rule 2: delete b between two vowels.

Step 4: why the order matters

Two orderings can be tested against the data.

Rule 3 before Rule 1. Take ‘search’, root asa. If we collapsed the vowels first, o + asa would become asa and the 2nd singular would look exactly like the imperative. It does not: it is wasa. So the o-to-w change must come first, turning o + asa into w + asa = wasa, and then there are no longer two vowels in a row for Rule 1 to touch.

Rule 1 before Rule 2. Take ‘get’, root bata, 3rd singular aata. If we deleted the b first we would get a-a-ta, and Rule 1 would then collapse the two a's into ata — the wrong answer. Applying Rule 1 first (there are no adjacent vowels in a + bata, so nothing happens) and only then deleting the b gives aata, which is correct. So the order is Rule 3, Rule 1, Rule 2.

A second, equally good analysis

The official solution accepts a mirror-image account: the 2nd-singular prefix is w- rather than o-, and the third rule instead changes w to o before a consonant (w + kamba gives okamba, while w + asa stays wasa). With that version the order is Rule 1, Rule 3, Rule 2. Either analysis predicts exactly the same forms, so both are marked correct — but you must keep one story consistent, not mix the two.

Step 5: filling in the table

First recover the root from whatever form is given, then rebuild the others.

  • ‘add’: imperative bakisa, so the root is bakisa. o + bakisa: the b is between o and a, so it drops, giving oakisa; a + bakisa gives aakisa; ba + bakisa gives baakisa.
  • ‘begin’: the 2nd singular wanda shows a w before a vowel, so the root begins with a vowel: anda. The imperative is therefore anda. a + anda collapses to anda; ba + anda collapses to banda.
  • ‘cure’: the 2nd singular is oowa. If the root started with a vowel we would expect a w, so the root must start with b whose deletion left the two o's: root bowa. Then a + bowa gives aowa and ba + bowa gives baowa.
  • ‘turn’: the 3rd singular aalusa has two a's, which means a b was deleted: root balusa. Hence the 2nd singular oalusa and the 3rd plural baalusa.
  • ‘chat’, ‘elect’ and ‘win’ start with s, p and l, so nothing is deleted or changed at all: just add o-, a- and ba-.
_reviewNotes: Answer keys taken from the official 2-page solution. A1 has TWO accepted analyses: (1) Ø-, (2) o- / w-, (3) a-, (4) ba-, (5) vowels, (6) the first one, (7) b, (8) vowels, (9) o / w, (10) w / o, (11) vowel / consonant, (12) 3 / 1, (13) 1 / 3, (14) 2. The alternates are listed as acceptedVariants on blanks 2, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, so a mixed-analysis answer would also be accepted by the auto-grader; a human may wish to check internal consistency. Special characters to verify against the PDF: Ø (blank 1 key and body text), ŋ in saŋga/loŋga/oloŋga/aloŋga/baloŋga, ɛ in ɛna/wɛna/bɛna, and d͡ʒ (d + combining double inverted breve U+0361 + ʒ) in imed͡ʒa, wimed͡ʒa, bimed͡ʒa, d͡ʒila, od͡ʒila, ad͡ʒila, bad͡ʒila. Point split: 14 A1 blanks at 0.14 (1.96) + 19 A2 blanks at 0.16 (3.04) = 5.00; the booklet gives no per-blank breakdown.
